title: Get them talking
desc: Speaking is where English grows fastest and where most classrooms give the least time. Sentence frames by level, structured pair talk, wait time, and how to ask a question a level-one student can answer.

cues.text: Every Teacher, from EL Publishing. Marcus, biology. Elena, EL specialist. Episode three. Elena, you said the fastest growth is in speaking. Why is that?

Because speaking is where the student finds out what they can and can't say yet. Reading and listening are receptive: you can nod along and think you've got it. Speaking is where the gap shows up, in real time, and gets closed. It's also the domain students use the most socially, so it grows on its own. What doesn't grow on its own is academic speaking: explaining a process, giving a reason, disagreeing with evidence. That has to be practiced in class, and in most classes, it's practiced about zero minutes a day.
So how much should it be?
In a ninety-minute block, I'd want ten minutes of structured student talk. Not a free-for-all. Structured. Partners, a question, a frame, a time limit, and a job for each person.
Let's start with the frame. I hear sentence frames a lot. What is one, and why does it work?

A sentence frame is the sentence with the content missing. The mitochondria produces blank. I think this is a plant cell because blank. The frame carries the grammar, so the student only has to supply the idea. For a level one, that means they can participate in a discussion they'd otherwise sit out. For a level four, you use the frame to push them into more complex language than they'd produce on their own. Although blank, the evidence suggests blank. They wouldn't say that on their own. With the frame, they will.
So different frames for different levels.

Four lanes. Level one: a frame with one blank and a word bank. This is a blank. Level two: a frame with two blanks, or a choice. The cell is a plant cell because it has a blank. Level three: a frame with a reason. I think blank because blank. Level four: a frame with a connector. Blank, however, blank. Or, the evidence that blank is blank. Put all four on the board. Let students pick. They'll usually pick the right one for themselves, and when they pick too low, you nudge.
Where do I get the frames?

You write them from your own content, which takes about two minutes once you've seen a few. Or there's a Sentence-Frame Bank on the hub, sorted by what you're trying to get them to do: describe, compare, explain, argue. Pull from that.
Okay, the structure. Walk me through ten minutes of pair talk that doesn't fall apart.

Here's the routine. One: the question is on the board, and so are the frames. Two: give thinking time. Thirty seconds of silence, students can write a word or two. Three: partner A talks for one minute, partner B listens and then says back one thing they heard. You said blank. Four: switch. Five: you pull two or three answers for the whole class, and you pick who, so it's not the same four hands every time. That's seven or eight minutes, and every student has spoken academic English twice.
The say-it-back part. Why that?
Because listening is half of talking. And because it protects the newcomer. If a level one student says a word, and their partner has to repeat it, the word was heard. It counted. Nobody got ignored.
You said give thinking time. I think I give about one second.

Everybody gives about one second. The research number is that teachers wait less than a second before calling on someone or answering their own question. For an English learner, that one second is spent translating the question. Count to five in your head. It feels like forever. It isn't. The quality of the answers goes up for every student in the room, not just the English learners.
How do I ask a question a level one can actually answer out loud?

Make the answer small and make the question carry the words. Instead of, what does the nucleus do, ask, does the nucleus control the cell, or store energy. Now the student has the words. They say, control the cell. That's a correct, spoken answer in academic English. Next week you ask, what does the nucleus do, and they've heard themselves say it before.
Choices. Yes or no. Either or.
And pointing. And finish my sentence. The nucleus controls the. And they say, cell. That's participation. It builds up.
What about pairing? The default is to sit the newcomer next to a kid who speaks Spanish.

That's fine for the first two weeks, as a bridge. It's not a plan. After that, rotate partners. The student needs to talk to English speakers, and the English speakers need to learn to talk to them. One rule that helps: the partner's job is not to translate. The partner's job is to say it slower and show it. If they translate, the newcomer never has to listen in English.
What do I stop worrying about?

Stop correcting pronunciation in front of the class. If the meaning was clear, let it go. If a word was wrong, say the right sentence back naturally. The student says, the cell have a nucleus. You say, yes, the cell has a nucleus, good. That's the correction. They heard it. Nobody got embarrassed. And a student who is embarrassed stops talking, which is the one thing we can't afford.
Next time: reading in the content area, which is where my level fours are stalling. Every Teacher is from EL Publishing. Free at radan55 dot github dot io slash everyteacher.
